text: Performance Troubleshooting's Instance Health Dashboard and Semaphore and Node Usage lesson show today's load on the platform — how contended the semaphore pool is right now. Capacity planning takes that same data and asks a different question: at the user count and data volume this instance will reach in twelve months, will today's configuration still hold up? That's projection, not reaction, and it's the architect's job, not the admin's.

Real capacity planning tracks two separate kinds of growth, because they strain different parts of the platform. User growth strains node capacity and semaphore pools directly, since every active session competes for the same limited pool. Data growth strains query performance and storage, which is why table design and archiving strategy matter. A rollout can triple one dimension while the other stays flat, so an architect projects both separately.

A fixed number of semaphores serves a fixed number of concurrent transactions, and once demand exceeds supply, requests start queuing — the exact symptom Performance Troubleshooting's Scheduled Job Contention lesson exists to diagnose. An architect runs that same math forward against a growth projection before the queuing starts. If usage is projected to double and the semaphore pool is already near capacity today, that contention is a near-certainty to plan for now, not a future maybe to monitor for later.

Projection without real data is guesswork. A practical capacity plan establishes concrete metrics — active user count by month, record growth in core tables, average and peak semaphore utilization — pulled from the Instance Health Dashboard, reviewed on a fixed cadence rather than only when things feel slow.

That cadence, commonly quarterly or ahead of any known rollout, turns capacity planning from a one-time estimate made at project kickoff into an ongoing discipline that catches a wrong projection early, while there's still time to act on it.
Track growth, set a cadence, act on the trend before contention becomes a queue. Next up: the performance architecture lab, working through a real three-times growth scenario end to end.
